name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm test -- --reporter=default --reporter=json --outputFile.json="$RUNNER_TEMP/vitest.json"
      - name: Slowest test files
        env:
          REPORT: ${{ runner.temp }}/vitest.json
        run: |
          node --input-type=module <<'EOF'
          import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
          const limit = 10;
          const root = process.cwd().replaceAll("\\", "/") + "/";
          const files = JSON.parse(readFileSync(process.env.REPORT, "utf8")).testResults
            .map(f => ({ file: f.name.replace(root, ""), seconds: (f.endTime - f.startTime) / 1000 }))
            .sort((a, b) => b.seconds - a.seconds);
          console.log("Slowest 10 test files:");
          for (const f of files.slice(0, 10)) console.log(`${f.seconds.toFixed(2).padStart(7)} s  ${f.file}`);
          const slow = files.filter(f => f.seconds > limit);
          for (const f of slow) console.log(`::error file=${f.file}::${f.file} took ${f.seconds.toFixed(1)} s; a test file may take at most ${limit} s. Split it, or mock the slow part (AGENTS.md Tests).`);
          if (slow.length) process.exit(1);
          EOF
      - run: npm run build
      - run: npm run check:bundle

  database:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Start the test backend
        run: |
          for attempt in 1 2 3 4; do
            npm run setup -- --qa && exit 0
            echo "::warning::Starting the test backend failed (attempt $attempt); the image registry limits pulls. Trying again."
            sleep $((attempt * 30))
          done
          exit 1
      - run: npm run test:db

  browser:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 25
    env:
      E2E_PRODUCTION_BUILD: "1"
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Start the test backend
        run: |
          for attempt in 1 2 3 4; do
            npm run setup -- --qa && exit 0
            echo "::warning::Starting the test backend failed (attempt $attempt); the image registry limits pulls. Trying again."
            sleep $((attempt * 30))
          done
          exit 1
      - run: npm run qa:auth
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - name: Browser journeys
        run: npm run test:e2e -- --workers=1 --retries=1 e2e/net-worth.gated.spec.ts e2e/import-journey.mocked.spec.ts
      - name: Upload failure traces and screenshots
        if: failure()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: browser-failures
          path: test-results/
          retention-days: 7
          if-no-files-found: ignore
name: Desktop

# Builds Moneo Desktop on Windows, macOS and Linux, smoke-tests the packaged app, and on a `v*` tag
# drafts a GitHub release with the installers. Packages are unsigned unless the signing secrets exist.

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "desktop/**"
      - "scripts/desktop/**"
      - "next.config.ts"
      - "package*.json"
      - "supabase/migrations/**"
      - ".github/workflows/desktop.yml"
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: desktop-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  build:
    name: ${{ matrix.id }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    timeout-minutes: 60
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - { id: win-x64, runner: windows-latest, builder: "--win --x64" }
          - { id: mac-arm64, runner: macos-15, builder: "--mac --arm64" }
          # macos-13 was retired; macos-15-intel is the remaining Intel runner, so mac-x64 builds
          # and is smoke-tested natively.
          - { id: mac-x64, runner: macos-15-intel, builder: "--mac --x64" }
          - { id: linux-x64, runner: ubuntu-24.04, builder: "--linux --x64" }
    defaults:
      run:
        shell: bash
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Check release version
        if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
        env:
          TAG: ${{ github.ref_name }}
        run: |
          version=$(node -p "require('./desktop/package.json').version")
          if [ "$TAG" != "v$version" ]; then
            echo "::error::Tag $TAG does not match desktop/package.json version $version."
            exit 1
          fi

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm

      # No setup-go: fetch-backend.mjs downloads its own pinned Go toolchain into desktop/.cache.
      - run: npm ci

      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: desktop/.cache
          key: desktop-cache-${{ matrix.id }}-${{ hashFiles('scripts/desktop/fetch-backend.mjs') }}

      - name: Fetch the native backend
        run: node scripts/desktop/fetch-backend.mjs --platform ${{ matrix.id }}

      - run: npm run desktop:build

      - name: Package
        env:
          CSC_LINK: ${{ secrets.CSC_LINK }}
          CSC_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.CSC_KEY_PASSWORD }}
          APPLE_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_ID }}
          APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD }}
          APPLE_TEAM_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_TEAM_ID }}
          WIN_CSC_LINK: ${{ secrets.WIN_CSC_LINK }}
          WIN_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.WIN_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD }}
          # electron-builder skips signing on pull requests; sign (ad hoc without a certificate) so
          # codesign's checks fail here instead of first on a release tag.
          CSC_FOR_PULL_REQUEST: "true"
        run: |
          # Secrets that do not exist arrive as empty strings; unset them so electron-builder
          # treats the build as unsigned.
          for name in CSC_LINK CSC_KEY_PASSWORD APPLE_ID APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD APPLE_TEAM_ID WIN_CSC_LINK WIN_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD; do
            if [ -z "${!name}" ]; then unset "$name"; fi
          done
          if [ -z "${CSC_LINK:-}" ] && [ -z "${WIN_CSC_LINK:-}" ]; then
            export CSC_IDENTITY_AUTO_DISCOVERY=false
            echo "No signing certificate: building unsigned packages."
          fi
          npm run desktop:dist -- ${{ matrix.builder }} --publish never
          # Both Mac jobs write latest-mac.yml. Macs only read the version from it (unsigned apps
          # download from the release page), so the Apple Silicon one is kept.
          if [ "${{ matrix.id }}" = "mac-x64" ]; then rm -f desktop/release/latest-mac.yml; fi

      - name: List packages
        run: ls -la desktop/release

      # The smoke test starts the unpacked app (own temporary home, no cloud calls).
      - name: Linux dependencies for the smoke test
        if: runner.os == 'Linux'
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y xvfb libnss3-tools
          # Ubuntu 24.04 blocks the unprivileged user namespaces Chromium's sandbox needs.
          sudo sysctl -w kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0

      - name: Smoke test
        run: |
          mkdir -p smoke
          if [ "$RUNNER_OS" = "Linux" ]; then
            xvfb-run -a --server-args="-screen 0 1280x1024x24" npm run desktop:smoke 2>&1 | tee "smoke/smoke-${{ matrix.id }}.log"
          else
            npm run desktop:smoke 2>&1 | tee "smoke/smoke-${{ matrix.id }}.log"
          fi

      - name: Upload installers
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: moneo-desktop-${{ matrix.id }}
          path: |
            desktop/release/*.exe
            desktop/release/*.dmg
            desktop/release/*.zip
            desktop/release/*.AppImage
            desktop/release/*.deb
            desktop/release/*.blockmap
            desktop/release/latest*.yml
          if-no-files-found: warn
          retention-days: 7

      - name: Upload smoke logs
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: smoke-${{ matrix.id }}
          path: smoke/
          if-no-files-found: ignore
          retention-days: 3

  release:
    name: Draft release
    if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 15
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: moneo-desktop-*
          path: installers
          merge-multiple: true

      - name: Draft the release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          TAG: ${{ github.ref_name }}
        run: |
          version=$(node -p "require('./desktop/package.json').version")
          if [ "$TAG" != "v$version" ]; then
            echo "::error::Tag $TAG does not match desktop/package.json version $version."
            exit 1
          fi
          cd installers
          ls -la
          files=$(find . -maxdepth 1 -type f \( -name '*.exe' -o -name '*.dmg' -o -name '*.zip' -o -name '*.AppImage' -o -name '*.deb' -o -name '*.blockmap' -o -name 'latest*.yml' \) -printf '%f\n' | sort)
          if [ -z "$files" ]; then echo "::error::No installers were downloaded."; exit 1; fi
          # shellcheck disable=SC2086
          sha256sum $files > SHA256SUMS.txt
          cat SHA256SUMS.txt
          # shellcheck disable=SC2086
          gh release create "$TAG" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --draft --verify-tag \
            --title "Moneo Desktop $TAG" \
            --notes "Moneo Desktop $TAG. Packages are unsigned unless noted; check SHA256SUMS.txt." \
            $files SHA256SUMS.txt

name: Desktop

# Builds Moneo Desktop on Windows, macOS and Linux, smoke-tests the packaged app, and on a `v*` tag
# drafts a GitHub release with the installers. Packages are unsigned unless the signing secrets exist.

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "desktop/**"
      - "scripts/desktop/**"
      - "next.config.ts"
      - "package*.json"
      - "supabase/migrations/**"
      - ".github/workflows/desktop.yml"
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: desktop-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  build:
    name: ${{ matrix.id }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    timeout-minutes: 60
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - { id: win-x64, runner: windows-latest, builder: "--win --x64" }
          - { id: mac-arm64, runner: macos-15, builder: "--mac --arm64" }
          # macos-13 was retired; macos-15-intel is the remaining Intel runner, so mac-x64 builds
          # and is smoke-tested natively.
          - { id: mac-x64, runner: macos-15-intel, builder: "--mac --x64" }
          - { id: linux-x64, runner: ubuntu-24.04, builder: "--linux --x64" }
    defaults:
      run:
        shell: bash
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Check release version
        if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
        env:
          TAG: ${{ github.ref_name }}
        run: |
          version=$(node -p "require('./desktop/package.json').version")
          if [ "$TAG" != "v$version" ]; then
            echo "::error::Tag $TAG does not match desktop/package.json version $version."
            exit 1
          fi

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm

      # No setup-go: fetch-backend.mjs downloads its own pinned Go toolchain into desktop/.cache.
      - run: npm ci

      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: desktop/.cache
          key: desktop-cache-${{ matrix.id }}-${{ hashFiles('scripts/desktop/fetch-backend.mjs') }}

      - name: Fetch the native backend
        run: node scripts/desktop/fetch-backend.mjs --platform ${{ matrix.id }}

      - run: npm run desktop:build

      - name: Package
        env:
          CSC_LINK: ${{ secrets.CSC_LINK }}
          CSC_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.CSC_KEY_PASSWORD }}
          APPLE_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_ID }}
          APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD }}
          APPLE_TEAM_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_TEAM_ID }}
          WIN_CSC_LINK: ${{ secrets.WIN_CSC_LINK }}
          WIN_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.WIN_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD }}
          # electron-builder skips signing on pull requests; sign (ad hoc without a certificate) so
          # codesign's checks fail here instead of first on a release tag.
          CSC_FOR_PULL_REQUEST: "true"
        run: |
          # Secrets that do not exist arrive as empty strings; unset them so electron-builder
          # treats the build as unsigned.
          for name in CSC_LINK CSC_KEY_PASSWORD APPLE_ID APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD APPLE_TEAM_ID WIN_CSC_LINK WIN_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD; do
            if [ -z "${!name}" ]; then unset "$name"; fi
          done
          if [ -z "${CSC_LINK:-}" ] && [ -z "${WIN_CSC_LINK:-}" ]; then
            export CSC_IDENTITY_AUTO_DISCOVERY=false
            echo "No signing certificate: building unsigned packages."
          fi
          npm run desktop:dist -- ${{ matrix.builder }} --publish never
          # Both Mac jobs write latest-mac.yml. Macs only read the version from it (unsigned apps
          # download from the release page), so the Apple Silicon one is kept.
          if [ "${{ matrix.id }}" = "mac-x64" ]; then rm -f desktop/release/latest-mac.yml; fi

      - name: List packages
        run: ls -la desktop/release

      # The smoke test starts the unpacked app (own temporary home, no cloud calls).
      - name: Linux dependencies for the smoke test
        if: runner.os == 'Linux'
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y xvfb libnss3-tools
          # Ubuntu 24.04 blocks the unprivileged user namespaces Chromium's sandbox needs.
          sudo sysctl -w kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0

      - name: Smoke test
        run: |
          mkdir -p smoke
          if [ "$RUNNER_OS" = "Linux" ]; then
            xvfb-run -a --server-args="-screen 0 1280x1024x24" npm run desktop:smoke 2>&1 | tee "smoke/smoke-${{ matrix.id }}.log"
          else
            npm run desktop:smoke 2>&1 | tee "smoke/smoke-${{ matrix.id }}.log"
          fi

      - name: Upload installers
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: moneo-desktop-${{ matrix.id }}
          path: |
            desktop/release/*.exe
            desktop/release/*.dmg
            desktop/release/*.zip
            desktop/release/*.AppImage
            desktop/release/*.deb
            desktop/release/*.blockmap
            desktop/release/latest*.yml
          if-no-files-found: warn
          retention-days: 7

      - name: Upload smoke logs
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: smoke-${{ matrix.id }}
          path: smoke/
          if-no-files-found: ignore
          retention-days: 3

  release:
    name: Draft release
    if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 15
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: moneo-desktop-*
          path: installers
          merge-multiple: true

      - name: Draft the release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          TAG: ${{ github.ref_name }}
        run: |
          version=$(node -p "require('./desktop/package.json').version")
          if [ "$TAG" != "v$version" ]; then
            echo "::error::Tag $TAG does not match desktop/package.json version $version."
            exit 1
          fi
          cd installers
          ls -la
          files=$(find . -maxdepth 1 -type f \( -name '*.exe' -o -name '*.dmg' -o -name '*.zip' -o -name '*.AppImage' -o -name '*.deb' -o -name '*.blockmap' -o -name 'latest*.yml' \) -printf '%f\n' | sort)
          if [ -z "$files" ]; then echo "::error::No installers were downloaded."; exit 1; fi
          # shellcheck disable=SC2086
          sha256sum $files > SHA256SUMS.txt
          cat SHA256SUMS.txt
          # shellcheck disable=SC2086
          gh release create "$TAG" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --draft --verify-tag \
            --title "Moneo Desktop $TAG" \

1	# Making OpenClaw CI faster and 95% cheaper · Vincent Koc
2	
3	https://vincent.build/openclaw-ci-cost-reduction/
4	
5	!ci-article-artwork-v2.png
6	
7	When I first talked about the dark factory—agents building software with other agents—people laughed. More people are now using agents this way. Ours ran into a different limit: not tokens, memory or disk, but tests.
8	
9	Agents were producing code faster. They were also producing more tests, more jobs and more retries. Work piled up while we waited for checks to show that changes were safe to ship. We had a hard deadline to reduce how much compute we needed.
10	
11	About **89% of our code is TypeScript**.1 That is where I began with faster tools and adaptive testing. The broader lessons—remove weak tests, balance work and stop repeating setup—apply across languages.
12	
13	Our Blacksmith runners logged **158,546 hours** in the September peak week and **21,395 hours** in the latest week: **86.5% less runtime**. The estimated value of that compute fell **95.5%**. Blacksmith sponsored the capacity—we did not pay those dollar amounts. The workload also changed, so neither reduction belongs to one fix. Here is what we changed: fewer pointless checks, better use of each machine and tests that adapt.
14	
15	### Try this with your agent
16	
17	Short on time? Send your agent this page and the OpenClaw CI implementation, then give it this prompt:
18	
19	```
20	Read https://vincent.build/openclaw-ci-cost-reduction/ and its linked OpenClaw CI implementation. Audit this repository’s CI and measure a baseline. Propose the highest-value changes, then implement them in reviewable steps. Preserve required checks; run the full suite when affected-test selection is uncertain. Verify correctness, feedback time and compute cost. Don’t assume OpenClaw’s tools or results transfer unchanged.
21	```
22	
23	## Who runs the tests, and what we measured
24	
25	GitHub Actions coordinates the work: which jobs run, their dependencies and their results. A runner is the machine doing that work. We use Blacksmith (and more recently, boat.dev) to supply those runners on top of GitHub Actions.
26	
27	Thank you to GitHub for supporting OpenClaw with donated CI runners and a GitHub Enterprise plan.
28	
29	Blacksmith sponsors these runners. Thank you to their team for making this work possible.
30	
31	Value of sponsored compute · Blacksmith**95.5% lower estimated compute value**
32	Measured17–23 Sep vs 6–13 Nov 2026USD / 30 days
33	USD per 30 days · based on each week’s daily average2
34	**$1,268,958per 30 days**
35	**$57,324per 30 days**
36	**95.5%**lower compute value**$1.21m less**per 30 days
37	**Heaviest week**17–23 Sep 2026
38	**Latest week**6–13 Nov 2026
39	Estimated value of Blacksmith-sponsored compute across the organization at published prices. Same scale and zero. Heaviest: 17 Sep 00:00–24 Sep 00:00 UTC. Latest: 6 Nov 09:00–13 Nov 09:00 UTC. Measurement notes · Source arithmetic.
40	
41	### What ran on those machines
42	
43	| Weekly usage | 17–23 September | 6–13 November |
44	| --- | --- | --- |
45	| Runner-hours | 158,546 | 21,395 |
46	| Jobs | 1,482,257 | 301,413 |
47	| Jobs per hour, average | 8,823 | 1,794 |
48	| Equivalent runners busy all week | 944 | 127 |
49	
50	That is **86.5% fewer runner-hours** and **79.7% fewer jobs**. The September total is enough runtime to keep **944 runners busy around the clock** for a week; the latest total is equivalent to **127**. That is runner-hours divided by the 168 hours in each week, not peak concurrency. Runner sizes varied.
51	
52	For another measure of scale, the main repository’s PR-triggered `CI` workflow ran **19,660 times** during 17–23 September—about **117 workflow runs an hour**. A workflow can fan out into many jobs. That count covers one workflow in one repository; the Blacksmith totals above cover all repositories on the account.
53	
54	All repositories on our Blacksmith account; all outcomes. Heaviest: 17 Sep 00:00–24 Sep 00:00 UTC. Latest: 6 Nov 09:00–13 Nov 09:00 UTC. Hours rounded from recorded runtime minutes. The workload changed between weeks; this is not the same work replayed on two CI setups. Source arithmetic.
55	
56	Activity fell too: indexed commits in the main repository were about **44% lower** across the comparison weeks (3,850 → 2,149). That is one repository against organization-wide cost, with slightly different daily boundaries, so it is context—not a saving measured at equal activity levels. Counting method.
57	
58	At Blacksmith’s published prices, keeping up the September week’s usage for 30 days would mean **$1.27 million worth of compute**. At the latest week’s usage, it would be **$57,324**2.
59	
60	A faster runner is useful, but it cannot fix poorly divided work. If each job spends most of its time preparing to run, buying faster execution tackles the smaller part of the problem. Our next step was to look at what we were asking those machines to do.
61	
62	The workload changed over this period too. The chart measures the combined result, not a saving we can assign to each fix. We also need to know how quickly changes get checked, reviewed and merged.
63	
64	The methods below are not tied to Blacksmith. We used its runners, but removing duplicate work, choosing relevant tests, reusing setup and balancing jobs apply to hosted runners and machines you operate yourself. The TypeScript examples show where we started, not where the ideas stop.
65	
66	## The goal: finish changes sooner
67	
68	I call this measure **agent cycle time: PR creation to merge**. It measures elapsed time for work done with agents, not every aspect of software quality.
69	
70	Writing the patch is only part of that interval. A PR can wait for a runner, install the same dependencies again, run an oversized suite, fail, get fixed and repeat. Review adds another wait. If another agent needs that change, that agent has to wait too.
71	
72	We have one objective: **finish useful work sooner, with less compute wasted along the way**. The first question is whether the work needs to run at all. Only then should we optimize the work that remains. A cheaper machine is not a win if it makes every dependent agent wait much longer. A faster machine is not a win if most of it sits idle.
73	
74	Removing unnecessary work can improve both. The job that never needed to start costs nothing and holds nobody up.
75	
76	Cost × time The tradeoff—and a real example
77	Illustrative goal + reported pairSame 240 test filesUSD / job · elapsed time
78	Read both charts the same way: left costs less; down finishes sooner.
79	**Ideal scenario**
80	LESS COST · LESS WAITING
81	Cost and time: lower-left improves bothSchematic, not measurements. Less cost. Less waiting. Cost increases right; elapsed time increases upward.Cheaperbut slowerCostlierand slowerCheaperAND fasterFasterbut costlierMORE WAIT TIME ↑← LESS COSTMORE COST →Starting point
82	**Less cost. Less waiting.**
83	Removing duplicated setup or unnecessary work can improve both. This is the goal—not a measured fleetwide result.
84	**What happened on one job**
85	REPORTED PAIR · SAME 240 FILES
86	Measured runner cost and elapsed timeSame 240-file job: 32-class costs 1.152 dollars and takes 17 minutes 54 seconds. 16-class costs 0.672 dollars and takes 20 minutes 51 seconds. Cost falls 41.7 percent and time rises 16.5 percent. Both share a known failure.$0.0$0.4$0.8$1.20 min10 min20 minBetter at bothrelative to 32-classMORE ELAPSED TIME (MIN) ↑← LESS COSTMORE COST →32-class16-class
87	**41.7% cheaper. 16.5% slower.**
88	32-class: $1.152 · 17m 54s.
89	16-class: $0.672 · 20m 51s.
90	The smaller runner lowered the estimated cost but added almost three minutes to the wait.
91	Left: the ideal direction, not measured savings. Right: one paired job from PR #167021; both runs share a known failure. Estimated cost at published prices and whole-job time, not a fleetwide result or PR-to-merge time.
92	
93	Every optimization needs a tradeoff check. Making a runner cheaper can make people—and other agents—wait longer. Adding parallel jobs can shorten the wait while repeating setup and increasing the estimated cost. Removing unnecessary work can improve both, but only if it really is unnecessary and sits on the path to an answer. Deleting code is not proof that the system got better.
94	
95	Start by removing unnecessary work, then measure what remains. Keep the behavior we need to protect, compare equivalent jobs, and look at cost and waiting time together.
96	
97	The reduction in estimated compute value is measured; the PR-to-merge improvement is not yet established here. Lower estimated costs alone do not prove that more changes get finished. That needs comparable delivery and work-volume measurements, not just a count of commits. Measurement notes.
98	
99	## 1. Delete the waste before optimizing it
100	
101	A test is useful when it catches a mistake we care about. More test code is not automatically more protection. My starting assumption in an agent-grown suite is that most tiny, implementation-mirroring unit tests are noise until they can demonstrate an independent contract. By noise I mean tests that restate the implementation, fail during harmless refactors, or stay green when the behavior they claim to protect is broken.
102	
103	Models are very good at adding code. My reading: adding a test looks thorough; deleting one means showing that nothing useful is lost. Ask for a fix and it is easy to get another fixture, another mock and five assertions for behavior another suite already proves. Deletion needs an explicit instruction and a place in the definition of done. Otherwise the suite keeps growing even when the product barely changes.
104	
105	Make every test earn its place before buying it a faster machine. Speeding up noise leaves the maintenance problem intact.
106	
107	Our cleanup worked one subsystem at a time. Read the production code and its tests. Name the contract. Find the strongest test that proves it. Only then remove duplication—or repair a test that proves nothing.
108	
109	### Set a limit on test-code growth
110	
111	We put that pressure into a guard, not just a prompt. The original test-line ratchet told an over-budget change to **“Offset the added lines by deleting or consolidating tests elsewhere”**, or justify a higher ceiling. The rule was: once the suite is at its ceiling, further test lines must be offset by deletion or consolidation, or the ceiling must be raised with a stated justification. That was the 24 October guard. It is a limit on the amount of test code, not a reason to delete useful product code or the only regression test.
112	
113	The rule evolved. By the 13 November checkpoint, the per-change policy allows **400 net new test lines** without an allocation record; larger additions need a recorded, justified allowance. So it is not a blanket one-line-in, one-line-out rule. The principle survives: make growth visible, make exceptions explicit, and reward consolidation. Original guard · Versioned budget.
114	
115	### After the cleanup, how much core code is tests?
116	
117	Focus on OpenClaw’s core, not every app and extension in the repository. At the article’s 13 November checkpoint, test files account for **56.5%** of counted core code. Test support adds **6.7%**, taking the combined share to **63.2%**. The remaining **36.8%** is implementation.
118	
119	OpenClaw core · 13 November 2026**Tests vs implementation**

# Making OpenClaw CI faster and 95% cheaper · Vincent Koc

https://vincent.build/openclaw-ci-cost-reduction/

!ci-article-artwork-v2.png

When I first talked about the dark factory—agents building software with other agents—people laughed. More people are now using agents this way. Ours ran into a different limit: not tokens, memory or disk, but tests.

Agents were producing code faster. They were also producing more tests, more jobs and more retries. Work piled up while we waited for checks to show that changes were safe to ship. We had a hard deadline to reduce how much compute we needed.

About **89% of our code is TypeScript**.1 That is where I began with faster tools and adaptive testing. The broader lessons—remove weak tests, balance work and stop repeating setup—apply across languages.

Our Blacksmith runners logged **158,546 hours** in the September peak week and **21,395 hours** in the latest week: **86.5% less runtime**. The estimated value of that compute fell **95.5%**. Blacksmith sponsored the capacity—we did not pay those dollar amounts. The workload also changed, so neither reduction belongs to one fix. Here is what we changed: fewer pointless checks, better use of each machine and tests that adapt.

### Try this with your agent

Short on time? Send your agent this page and the OpenClaw CI implementation, then give it this prompt:

```
Read https://vincent.build/openclaw-ci-cost-reduction/ and its linked OpenClaw CI implementation. Audit this repository’s CI and measure a baseline. Propose the highest-value changes, then implement them in reviewable steps. Preserve required checks; run the full suite when affected-test selection is uncertain. Verify correctness, feedback time and compute cost. Don’t assume OpenClaw’s tools or results transfer unchanged.
```

## Who runs the tests, and what we measured

GitHub Actions coordinates the work: which jobs run, their dependencies and their results. A runner is the machine doing that work. We use Blacksmith (and more recently, boat.dev) to supply those runners on top of GitHub Actions.

Thank you to GitHub for supporting OpenClaw with donated CI runners and a GitHub Enterprise plan.

Blacksmith sponsors these runners. Thank you to their team for making this work possible.

### What ran on those machines

That is **86.5% fewer runner-hours** and **79.7% fewer jobs**. The September total is enough runtime to keep **944 runners busy around the clock** for a week; the latest total is equivalent to **127**. That is runner-hours divided by the 168 hours in each week, not peak concurrency. Runner sizes varied.

For another measure of scale, the main repository’s PR-triggered `CI` workflow ran **19,660 times** during 17–23 September—about **117 workflow runs an hour**. A workflow can fan out into many jobs. That count covers one workflow in one repository; the Blacksmith totals above cover all repositories on the account.

All repositories on our Blacksmith account; all outcomes. Heaviest: 17 Sep 00:00–24 Sep 00:00 UTC. Latest: 6 Nov 09:00–13 Nov 09:00 UTC. Hours rounded from recorded runtime minutes. The workload changed between weeks; this is not the same work replayed on two CI setups. Source arithmetic.

Activity fell too: indexed commits in the main repository were about **44% lower** across the comparison weeks (3,850 → 2,149). That is one repository against organization-wide cost, with slightly different daily boundaries, so it is context—not a saving measured at equal activity levels. Counting method.

At Blacksmith’s published prices, keeping up the September week’s usage for 30 days would mean **$1.27 million worth of compute**. At the latest week’s usage, it would be **$57,324**2.

A faster runner is useful, but it cannot fix poorly divided work. If each job spends most of its time preparing to run, buying faster execution tackles the smaller part of the problem. Our next step was to look at what we were asking those machines to do.

The workload changed over this period too. The chart measures the combined result, not a saving we can assign to each fix. We also need to know how quickly changes get checked, reviewed and merged.

The methods below are not tied to Blacksmith. We used its runners, but removing duplicate work, choosing relevant tests, reusing setup and balancing jobs apply to hosted runners and machines you operate yourself. The TypeScript examples show where we started, not where the ideas stop.

## The goal: finish changes sooner

I call this measure **agent cycle time: PR creation to merge**. It measures elapsed time for work done with agents, not every aspect of software quality.

Writing the patch is only part of that interval. A PR can wait for a runner, install the same dependencies again, run an oversized suite, fail, get fixed and repeat. Review adds another wait. If another agent needs that change, that agent has to wait too.

We have one objective: **finish useful work sooner, with less compute wasted along the way**. The first question is whether the work needs to run at all. Only then should we optimize the work that remains. A cheaper machine is not a win if it makes every dependent agent wait much longer. A faster machine is not a win if most of it sits idle.

Removing unnecessary work can improve both. The job that never needed to start costs nothing and holds nobody up.

Every optimization needs a tradeoff check. Making a runner cheaper can make people—and other agents—wait longer. Adding parallel jobs can shorten the wait while repeating setup and increasing the estimated cost. Removing unnecessary work can improve both, but only if it really is unnecessary and sits on the path to an answer. Deleting code is not proof that the system got better.

Start by removing unnecessary work, then measure what remains. Keep the behavior we need to protect, compare equivalent jobs, and look at cost and waiting time together.

The reduction in estimated compute value is measured; the PR-to-merge improvement is not yet established here. Lower estimated costs alone do not prove that more changes get finished. That needs comparable delivery and work-volume measurements, not just a count of commits. Measurement notes.

## 1. Delete the waste before optimizing it

A test is useful when it catches a mistake we care about. More test code is not automatically more protection. My starting assumption in an agent-grown suite is that most tiny, implementation-mirroring unit tests are noise until they can demonstrate an independent contract. By noise I mean tests that restate the implementation, fail during harmless refactors, or stay green when the behavior they claim to protect is broken.

Models are very good at adding code. My reading: adding a test looks thorough; deleting one means showing that nothing useful is lost. Ask for a fix and it is easy to get another fixture, another mock and five assertions for behavior another suite already proves. Deletion needs an explicit instruction and a place in the definition of done. Otherwise the suite keeps growing even when the product barely changes.

Make every test earn its place before buying it a faster machine. Speeding up noise leaves the maintenance problem intact.

Our cleanup worked one subsystem at a time. Read the production code and its tests. Name the contract. Find the strongest test that proves it. Only then remove duplication—or repair a test that proves nothing.

### Set a limit on test-code growth

We put that pressure into a guard, not just a prompt. The original test-line ratchet told an over-budget change to **“Offset the added lines by deleting or consolidating tests elsewhere”**, or justify a higher ceiling. The rule was: once the suite is at its ceiling, further test lines must be offset by deletion or consolidation, or the ceiling must be raised with a stated justification. That was the 24 October guard. It is a limit on the amount of test code, not a reason to delete useful product code or the only regression test.

The rule evolved. By the 13 November checkpoint, the per-change policy allows **400 net new test lines** without an allocation record; larger additions need a recorded, justified allowance. So it is not a blanket one-line-in, one-line-out rule. The principle survives: make growth visible, make exceptions explicit, and reward consolidation. Original guard · Versioned budget.

### After the cleanup, how much core code is tests?

Focus on OpenClaw’s core, not every app and extension in the repository. At the article’s 13 November checkpoint, test files account for **56.5%** of counted core code. Test support adds **6.7%**, taking the combined share to **63.2%**. The remaining **36.8%** is implementation.

These are net changes between snapshots—not a count of every deletion, or savings attributed to one cleanup.

The test/spec category is not labelled “unit tests”: a file called `something.test.ts` can exercise a whole component. A full-release run also executes many of these same files; it is not an extra category of code. The chart measures the maintenance surface, not how much is waste or should be deleted.

Source report24 Sep 2026Original post
Peter’s reported cleanup, not a reconstructed test-LOC series. Open on X ↗

The test-audit rule is simple: name the behavior a test protects, show a believable bug that would make it fail, and keep one strong owner for that contract.

In one cleanup, a test checked that a result was a correctly formatted SHA-256 value, then separately checked that it did not contain the word `synthetic`. The format already ruled that word out. We removed the second assertion and kept the independent disclosure check. Deliberately breaking the code confirmed that the remaining guard still caught the bug. PR #191917.

All 12 test cases stayed. We removed duplicate work inside a test, not its independent protection.

### A cleanup goal you can reuse

Adapted from the cleanup goals I used for `libopus-wasm` and `libterminal`. It directs a repository-wide campaign, not a one-off audit or a superficial cleanup PR. Narrow PRs keep the work reviewable; the ledger keeps the agent moving through the whole scope.

```
/goal Run a sustained cleanup campaign across this repository's tests. Make every retained test earn its execution and maintenance cost.
Read each subsystem's production code before its tests. Identify the behavior contracts and realistic regressions worth protecting. Remove obsolete tests, implementation-mirroring assertions, duplicate coverage, unused fixtures and unnecessary mocks. Consolidate overlapping tests around the strongest behavior checks. Repair valuable flaky tests instead of preserving their retry tax.
Treat deletions and consolidation as first-class deliverables. Follow the repository’s test-line budget; justify genuinely new coverage rather than padding a replacement suite. Never offset growth by deleting an independent safety contract.
Do not stop after easy deletions or a small first PR. Work through every in-scope subsystem. Keep a ledger of completed areas, removed duplication, remaining contract coverage and unresolved risks; resume from it until the campaign is complete. Do not chase a deletion percentage or add replacement tests just to keep the count up.
For each change, run the affected checks and demonstrate that the retained test fails for the relevant broken behavior when practical. Never delete the only useful regression guard to make a failure disappear. Keep platform and integration boundaries that protect distinct behavior.
Validate and land narrow PRs within the repository's existing review and merge rules. Continue until every in-scope area is checked or has a precise blocker. No releases.
```

This is why the cleanup starts by reading the implementation, not sorting tests by runtime and deleting the slowest. Two similar-looking tests may protect different behavior; a very fast test may protect nothing useful. The question is what would break without it, and which remaining test would catch that break.

## 2. Put each check at the right stage

Not every check has to hold a PR open. We separated **the answer needed to merge this change** from **the broader proof needed to ship a release**.

What runs when**Every push is not a full release rehearsal.**
Workflow designEvent-basedNot measured durations
**PR revision**Checks required for this change*→***Answer before merge**
Selected tests, lint, types, security and review.
**Push to main**Small regression and protocol guards*→***Catch immediate breakage**
Full-suite replay can be disabled; small guards remain.
**Scheduled worker**Broader validation of a named main revision*→***Repair failures; qualify releases**
Hourly main validation; full release checks on its own schedule.
Versioned workflow design; the live full-CI switch was not verified. Required release evidence must match the version being shipped.

### Stop starting work that will be superseded

A busy agent can push the next revision before the previous one finishes starting. The old run gets cancelled; the new run repeats setup. Those cancelled runs used compute without producing a useful result.

Earlier in the campaign, the full main-push path gained a 90-second admission delay: a superseding push could cancel it before a Blacksmith runner started. That optimization preceded the separation of full validation from every main push. It was not a delay on PR feedback. The change.

We also moved main’s CodeQL analysis to an **hourly** schedule. A successful, unchanged category could reuse its result for up to 24 hours; changed, stale, failed or incomplete categories ran again. PR and manual security checks stayed. Scheduling · Reuse rules.

Moving a check changes when its answer is needed; it should not make a required answer optional.

### Stop the job before paying for its setup

A skip is worth more before the runner starts. The examples below trace six real workflow changes: a gate at the job condition avoids allocation and setup; a late check can only avoid the work after it. Put the decision at the earliest stage that has enough information to make it correctly.

Execution path Stop unnecessary jobs before setup starts
IllustrativeExecution stagesNot measured frequencies
What happened**1** decide to start**2** start machine**3** check details**4** install & setup**5** run the check
#188600 Comment with a linkNo machine startsstop2345
#191007 PR checks already passedNo failure-report job startsstop2345
#95308 Comment does not request a reviewNo review is started12stop45
#189132 Scheduled PR checkSkip an unnecessary GitHub request12stop45
#191805 CodeQL result is still validNo new scan starts12stop45
selection Tests without a selection ruleEvery test still runs1234runs
A stop at step 1 avoids starting a machine. A stop at step 3 has already paid to start one, but avoids later work. Dark cells are reached; pale cells are skipped. These examples show where work stops, not how often it happens.

### Do not rerun the full suite after every merge

The full suite does not need to restart after every commit lands on main. The versioned workflow separates three jobs: give the PR its required answer before merge, run small guards on each main push, and let a scheduled worker check broader combinations on a named revision.

Broader main validation runs hourly; full release validation has its own schedule. Full CI on every main push is opt-in in the source. Exact workflow and switch.

A background worker needs a clear obligation: qualify a named revision, retain its results, and report failures to whoever can repair them. Do not silently treat an old green run as proof for a newer commit. Keep release gates attached to the version being shipped. That is the operational work required to move tests out of the author's immediate wait.

We did not turn every background job into optional work. My rollout check was that releases did not suffer and full E2E runs did not reveal a new pattern of repeated regressions. That is an operational assessment, not a measured defect-rate claim.

- Source and configuration detail
    
    At the article’s source revision, `OPENCLAW_CI_ON_PUSH=true` enables the full main-push path. The workflow retains small main-push guards, schedules main CI hourly, and schedules full release validation separately. This describes the versioned design; the live repository-variable value was not available to this audit. CI source · Release validation source.
    

## 3. Stop paying for the same review twice

ClawSweeper is OpenClaw's automated maintenance and code-review bot. It reviews pull requests and reports findings so contributors and maintainers can act on them. It is another consumer of compute and attention, not a free step outside the delivery process.

ClawSweeper gives a new PR **one automatic review**. Follow-up reviews are requested, rather than automatically repeating the entire review after every push. Use a new review when the patch is ready for another pass or when a change needs fresh scrutiny; a request is not itself a passing review.

Its local-review CLI lets us inspect a branch on our own machines without allocating an Actions runner. The standalone AutoReview skill offers another local review workflow. Local describes where the tooling runs, not an offline model: both use their configured model service.

For a clean, committed branch, run this from a built ClawSweeper checkout, replacing the repository and path:

```
pnpm run review -- --local-range \
  --target-repo owner/repo --target-dir ../your-repo \
  --base origin/main
```

Or, with AutoReview installed, run from the repository you want reviewed:

```
python3 "$HOME/.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview" \
  --mode branch --base origin/main
```

The useful saving is avoiding redundant review starts and repeated findings while an author is still editing. Required CI, security checks and repository review rules remain. We did not move every review off CI, and no isolated review-cost percentage is claimed here.

## 4. Test the change, not the entire repository

Adaptive testing is the next step after cleanup: choose the remaining work from the change itself. Start with explicit ownership and dependencies. A changed test runs; a known production owner selects its related tests; shared, dynamic or uncertain paths widen the selection. A missing dependency record is a reason to run more, not evidence that nothing can break.

For our TypeScript-heavy repository, we began with the changed files, their owners and the code importing them. A change to one component should not automatically start tests for every unrelated component and platform.

For example, change a shared retry helper. Its own tests matter. So do tests of callers that import it. An unrelated UI component should not become relevant merely because it lives in the same repository. If we cannot establish the boundary safely, we run more.

Adaptive testing · one TypeScript change**Change the code. Run the tests it can affect.**
IllustrativeOne changed fileDependency-based selection
Changed source`retry.ts`Shared retry helper
Own test`retry.test.ts`Proves retry behavior**Run**
Imports the helper`send.ts`Message sender
Caller’s test`send.test.ts`Proves sender behavior**Run**
Unrelated test`profile.test.ts`No path to the change**Skipped**
Selection appears at step 4**retry.test.tssend.test.tsprofile.test.ts**
1 / 4
**Start with the changed file.**
retry.ts changed. That is the input to the selector—not a reason to run everything.
Illustrative files · no model call
Teaching example, not a captured run. Current ownership and imports select tests. Missing or ambiguous inputs widen the run; they never justify a skip.

Adaptive testing selects relevant tests, but smaller runs alone don’t prove complete coverage.

### Keep selection boring, deterministic and testable

We deliberately did not make this a complex AI scheduling system. Some teams use learned models or LLMs to choose tests. Our live path is ordinary code: the same revision, diff and rules produce the same selection. Every selected test should have a reason you can inspect. A model’s confidence is not a substitute for a dependency.

**Backtest the selector against regressions.** Take an earlier bug, restore the revision before its fix, and replay the change through the selector. Check whether it includes the test that exposes the bug, then run that test and verify the expected failure. Include deleted files, shared helpers, fixtures and renamed modules—not just easy sibling-test examples. A missed regression is a rule to repair or a reason to widen the fallback. This is a repeatable validation recipe, not a claim that we have replayed every historical bug.

### How we wired adaptive testing into CI

The implementation is a planner in front of the existing test runner. It turns a Git diff into a list of existing test files, then gives those files to their normal execution jobs.

**1. Start with an exact diff.** CI supplies the changed paths and comparison revision. Keep additions, deletions and rename information: removing a module can break its callers too. The planner also reads the current checkout and test inventory. A previous run’s dependency list is not a substitute for the code being tested now.

**2. Find the owning tests, then the callers.** In `test-projects.test-support.mts`, we map known inputs to explicit test owners, look for sibling and directory tests, and follow reverse imports to tests that consume the changed code. Package aliases are resolved as well. The aggressive PR policy bounds how far some searches go; it is not an unlimited walk through the repository. Changes to mocked exports have extra rules to retain affected mock consumers.

This is where the `retry.ts` example becomes real: select `retry.test.ts` because it owns the helper, and `send.test.ts` because its code consumes that helper. But an import graph cannot see every dependency. A test that reads a JSON fixture from disk needs an explicit owner rule or a recorded file dependency. “No import found” alone is not a reason to skip it.

**3. Add the checks the diff does not get to remove.** `ci-changed-node-test-plan.mts` combines the result with the applicable policy checks and fixed smoke tests. Changed tests remain eligible to run. Tests with protected owners follow their own rules. The small unchanged-input shortcut described below applies only to reviewed Markdown tests in directory fallback—not to every test that passed last time.

**4. Hand the selection to the existing runner.** The CI planner matches each selected file to its canonical test configuration, then constructs jobs with the appropriate runtime, setup and build requirements. Selecting the same file under Node and Bun still represents two executions. Missing executable owners or shard metadata cause the narrowed plan to be rejected, not treated as an empty successful test run. Broader coverage remains the fallback.

**5. Make the decision inspectable.** The selector records reasons such as `explicit-owner`, `import-consumer`, `policy-watch` and `fixed-smoke`. That lets us trace a surprising selection back to a rule. We check those rules with focused selector tests and regression examples; for the recorded-dependency pilot, we also deliberately broke a fixture and verified that the affected test was selected and failed. A smaller green run, by itself, cannot prove that selection is correct.

For local feedback, the repository exposes a changed-test command. Its defaults are not identical to the canonical CI planner; use the broader fallback when investigating a change that needs it:

```
pnpm test:changed
# With broad fallback
OPENCLAW_TEST_CHANGED_BROAD=1 \
  pnpm test:changed
```

name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm test -- --reporter=default --reporter=json --outputFile.json="$RUNNER_TEMP/vitest.json"
      - name: Slowest test files
        env:
          REPORT: ${{ runner.temp }}/vitest.json
        run: |
          node --input-type=module <<'EOF'
          import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
          const limit = 10;
          const root = process.cwd().replaceAll("\\", "/") + "/";
          const files = JSON.parse(readFileSync(process.env.REPORT, "utf8")).testResults
            .map(f => ({ file: f.name.replace(root, ""), seconds: (f.endTime - f.startTime) / 1000 }))
            .sort((a, b) => b.seconds - a.seconds);
          console.log("Slowest 10 test files:");
          for (const f of files.slice(0, 10)) console.log(`${f.seconds.toFixed(2).padStart(7)} s  ${f.file}`);
          const slow = files.filter(f => f.seconds > limit);
          for (const f of slow) console.log(`::error file=${f.file}::${f.file} took ${f.seconds.toFixed(1)} s; a test file may take at most ${limit} s. Split it, or mock the slow part (AGENTS.md Tests).`);
          if (slow.length) process.exit(1);
          EOF
      - run: npm run build
      - run: npm run check:bundle

  database:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Start the test backend
        run: |
          for attempt in 1 2 3 4; do
            npm run setup -- --qa && exit 0
            echo "::warning::Starting the test backend failed (attempt $attempt); the image registry limits pulls. Trying again."
            sleep $((attempt * 30))
          done
          exit 1
      - run: npm run test:db

  browser:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 25
    env:
      E2E_PRODUCTION_BUILD: "1"
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Start the test backend
        run: |
          for attempt in 1 2 3 4; do
            npm run setup -- --qa && exit 0
            echo "::warning::Starting the test backend failed (attempt $attempt); the image registry limits pulls. Trying again."
            sleep $((attempt * 30))
          done
          exit 1
      - run: npm run qa:auth
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - name: Browser journeys
        run: npm run test:e2e -- --workers=1 --retries=1 e2e/net-worth.gated.spec.ts e2e/import-journey.mocked.spec.ts
      - name: Upload failure traces and screenshots
        if: failure()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: browser-failures
          path: test-results/
          retention-days: 7
          if-no-files-found: ignore
name: Desktop

# Builds Moneo Desktop on Windows, macOS and Linux, smoke-tests the packaged app, and on a `v*` tag
# drafts a GitHub release with the installers. Packages are unsigned unless the signing secrets exist.

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "desktop/**"
      - "scripts/desktop/**"
      - "next.config.ts"
      - "package*.json"
      - "supabase/migrations/**"
      - ".github/workflows/desktop.yml"
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: desktop-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  build:
    name: ${{ matrix.id }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    timeout-minutes: 60
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - { id: win-x64, runner: windows-latest, builder: "--win --x64" }
          - { id: mac-arm64, runner: macos-15, builder: "--mac --arm64" }
          # macos-13 was retired; macos-15-intel is the remaining Intel runner, so mac-x64 builds
          # and is smoke-tested natively.
          - { id: mac-x64, runner: macos-15-intel, builder: "--mac --x64" }
          - { id: linux-x64, runner: ubuntu-24.04, builder: "--linux --x64" }
    defaults:
      run:
        shell: bash
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Check release version
        if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
        env:
          TAG: ${{ github.ref_name }}
        run: |
          version=$(node -p "require('./desktop/package.json').version")
          if [ "$TAG" != "v$version" ]; then
            echo "::error::Tag $TAG does not match desktop/package.json version $version."
            exit 1
          fi

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm

      # No setup-go: fetch-backend.mjs downloads its own pinned Go toolchain into desktop/.cache.
      - run: npm ci

      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: desktop/.cache
          key: desktop-cache-${{ matrix.id }}-${{ hashFiles('scripts/desktop/fetch-backend.mjs') }}

      - name: Fetch the native backend
        run: node scripts/desktop/fetch-backend.mjs --platform ${{ matrix.id }}

      - run: npm run desktop:build

      - name: Package
        env:
          CSC_LINK: ${{ secrets.CSC_LINK }}
          CSC_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.CSC_KEY_PASSWORD }}
          APPLE_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_ID }}
          APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD }}
          APPLE_TEAM_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_TEAM_ID }}
          WIN_CSC_LINK: ${{ secrets.WIN_CSC_LINK }}
          WIN_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.WIN_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD }}
          # electron-builder skips signing on pull requests; sign (ad hoc without a certificate) so
          # codesign's checks fail here instead of first on a release tag.
          CSC_FOR_PULL_REQUEST: "true"
        run: |
          # Secrets that do not exist arrive as empty strings; unset them so electron-builder
          # treats the build as unsigned.
          for name in CSC_LINK CSC_KEY_PASSWORD APPLE_ID APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD APPLE_TEAM_ID WIN_CSC_LINK WIN_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD; do
            if [ -z "${!name}" ]; then unset "$name"; fi
          done
          if [ -z "${CSC_LINK:-}" ] && [ -z "${WIN_CSC_LINK:-}" ]; then
            export CSC_IDENTITY_AUTO_DISCOVERY=false
            echo "No signing certificate: building unsigned packages."
          fi
          npm run desktop:dist -- ${{ matrix.builder }} --publish never
          # Both Mac jobs write latest-mac.yml. Macs only read the version from it (unsigned apps
          # download from the release page), so the Apple Silicon one is kept.
          if [ "${{ matrix.id }}" = "mac-x64" ]; then rm -f desktop/release/latest-mac.yml; fi

      - name: List packages
        run: ls -la desktop/release

      # The smoke test starts the unpacked app (own temporary home, no cloud calls).
      - name: Linux dependencies for the smoke test
        if: runner.os == 'Linux'
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y xvfb libnss3-tools
          # Ubuntu 24.04 blocks the unprivileged user namespaces Chromium's sandbox needs.
          sudo sysctl -w kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0

      - name: Smoke test
        run: |
          mkdir -p smoke
          if [ "$RUNNER_OS" = "Linux" ]; then
            xvfb-run -a --server-args="-screen 0 1280x1024x24" npm run desktop:smoke 2>&1 | tee "smoke/smoke-${{ matrix.id }}.log"
          else
            npm run desktop:smoke 2>&1 | tee "smoke/smoke-${{ matrix.id }}.log"
          fi

      - name: Upload installers
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: moneo-desktop-${{ matrix.id }}
          path: |
            desktop/release/*.exe
            desktop/release/*.dmg
            desktop/release/*.zip
            desktop/release/*.AppImage
            desktop/release/*.deb
            desktop/release/*.blockmap
            desktop/release/latest*.yml
          if-no-files-found: warn
          retention-days: 7

      - name: Upload smoke logs
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: smoke-${{ matrix.id }}
          path: smoke/
          if-no-files-found: ignore
          retention-days: 3

  release:
    name: Draft release
    if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 15
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: moneo-desktop-*
          path: installers
          merge-multiple: true

      - name: Draft the release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          TAG: ${{ github.ref_name }}
        run: |
          version=$(node -p "require('./desktop/package.json').version")
          if [ "$TAG" != "v$version" ]; then
            echo "::error::Tag $TAG does not match desktop/package.json version $version."
            exit 1
          fi
          cd installers
          ls -la
          files=$(find . -maxdepth 1 -type f \( -name '*.exe' -o -name '*.dmg' -o -name '*.zip' -o -name '*.AppImage' -o -name '*.deb' -o -name '*.blockmap' -o -name 'latest*.yml' \) -printf '%f\n' | sort)
          if [ -z "$files" ]; then echo "::error::No installers were downloaded."; exit 1; fi
          # shellcheck disable=SC2086
          sha256sum $files > SHA256SUMS.txt
          cat SHA256SUMS.txt
          # shellcheck disable=SC2086
          gh release create "$TAG" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --draft --verify-tag \
            --title "Moneo Desktop $TAG" \
            --notes "Moneo Desktop $TAG. Packages are unsigned unless noted; check SHA256SUMS.txt." \
            $files SHA256SUMS.txt

6	
7	When I first talked about the dark factory—agents building software with other agents—people laughed. More people are now using agents this way. Ours ran into a different limit: not tokens, memory or disk, but tests.
8	
9	Agents were producing code faster. They were also producing more tests, more jobs and more retries. Work piled up while we waited for checks to show that changes were safe to ship. We had a hard deadline to reduce how much compute we needed.

57	
58	At Blacksmith’s published prices, keeping up the September week’s usage for 30 days would mean **$1.27 million worth of compute**. At the latest week’s usage, it would be **$57,324**2.
59	
60	A faster runner is useful, but it cannot fix poorly divided work. If each job spends most of its time preparing to run, buying faster execution tackles the smaller part of the problem. Our next step was to look at what we were asking those machines to do.
61	
62	The workload changed over this period too. The chart measures the combined result, not a saving we can assign to each fix. We also need to know how quickly changes get checked, reviewed and merged.
63	
64	The methods below are not tied to Blacksmith. We used its runners, but removing duplicate work, choosing relevant tests, reusing setup and balancing jobs apply to hosted runners and machines you operate yourself. The TypeScript examples show where we started, not where the ideas stop.
65	
66	## The goal: finish changes sooner
67	
68	I call this measure **agent cycle time: PR creation to merge**. It measures elapsed time for work done with agents, not every aspect of software quality.
69	
70	Writing the patch is only part of that interval. A PR can wait for a runner, install the same dependencies again, run an oversized suite, fail, get fixed and repeat. Review adds another wait. If another agent needs that change, that agent has to wait too.
71	
72	We have one objective: **finish useful work sooner, with less compute wasted along the way**. The first question is whether the work needs to run at all. Only then should we optimize the work that remains. A cheaper machine is not a win if it makes every dependent agent wait much longer. A faster machine is not a win if most of it sits idle.
73	
74	Removing unnecessary work can improve both. The job that never needed to start costs nothing and holds nobody up.

92

Adding parallel jobs can shorten the wait while repeating setup and increasing the estimated cost. Removing unnecessary work can improve both, but only if it really is unnecessary and sits on the path to an answer. Deleting code is not proof that the system got better.
94	
95	Start by removing unnecessary work, then measure what remains. Keep the behavior we need to protect, compare equivalent jobs, and look at cost and waiting time together.
96	
97	The reduction in estimated compute value is measured; the PR-to-merge improvement is not yet established here. Lower estimated costs alone do not prove that more changes get finished. That needs comparable delivery and work-volume measurements, not just a count of commits. Measurement notes.
98	
99	## 1. Delete the waste before optimizing it
100	
101	A test is useful when it catches a mistake we care about. More test code is not automatically more protection. My starting assumption in an agent-grown suite is that most tiny, implementation-mirroring unit tests are noise until they can demonstrate an independent contract. By noise I mean tests that restate the implementation, fail during harmless refactors, or stay green when the behavior they claim to protect is broken.
102	
103	Models are very good at adding code. My reading: adding a test looks thorough; deleting one means showing that nothing useful is lost. Ask for a fix and it is easy to get another fixture, another mock and five assertions for behavior another suite already proves. Deletion needs an explicit instruction and a place in the definition of done. Otherwise the suite keeps growing even when the product barely changes.
104	
105	Make every test earn its place before buying it a faster machine. Speeding up noise leaves the maintenance problem intact.
106	
107	Our cleanup worked one subsystem at a time. Read the production code and its tests. Name the contract. Find the strongest test that proves it. Only then remove duplication—or repair a test that proves nothing.
108	
109	### Set a limit on test-code growth
110	
111	We put that pressure into a guard, not just a prompt. The original test-line ratchet told an over-budget change to **“Offset the added lines by deleting or consolidating tests elsewhere”**, or justify a higher ceiling. The rule was: once the suite is at its ceiling, further test lines must be offset by deletion or consolidation, or the ceiling must be raised with a stated justification. That was the 24 October guard. It is a limit on the amount of test code, not a reason to delete useful product code or the only regression test.
112	
113	The rule evolved. By the 13 November checkpoint, the per-change policy allows **400 net new test lines** without an allocation record; larger additions need a recorded, justified allowance. So it is not a blanket one-line-in, one-line-out rule. The principle survives: make growth visible, make exceptions explicit, and reward consolidation. Original guard · Versioned budget.
114

116	
117	Focus on OpenClaw’s core, not every app and extension in the repository. At the article’s 13 November checkpoint, test files account for **56.5%** of counted core code. Test support adds **6.7%**, taking the combined share to **63.2%**. The remaining **36.8%** is implementation.

141	
142	The test/spec category is not labelled “unit tests”: a file called `something.test.ts` can exercise a whole component. A full-release run also executes many of these same files; it is not an extra category of code. The chart measures the maintenance surface, not how much is waste or should be deleted.
143	
144	Source report24 Sep 2026Original post
