146	
147	The test-audit rule is simple: name the behavior a test protects, show a believable bug that would make it fail, and keep one strong owner for that contract.
148	
149	In one cleanup, a test checked that a result was a correctly formatted SHA-256 value, then separately checked that it did not contain the word `synthetic`. The format already ruled that word out. We removed the second assertion and kept the independent disclosure check. Deliberately breaking the code confirmed that the remaining guard still caught the bug. PR #191917.
150	
151	All 12 test cases stayed. We removed duplicate work inside a test, not its independent protection.
152	
153	### A cleanup goal you can reuse
154	
155	Adapted from the cleanup goals I used for `libopus-wasm` and `libterminal`. It directs a repository-wide campaign, not a one-off audit or a superficial cleanup PR. Narrow PRs keep the work reviewable; the ledger keeps the agent moving through the whole scope.
156	
157	```
158	/goal Run a sustained cleanup campaign across this repository's tests. Make every retained test earn its execution and maintenance cost.
159	Read each subsystem's production code before its tests. Identify the behavior contracts and realistic regressions worth protecting. Remove obsolete tests, implementation-mirroring assertions, duplicate coverage, unused fixtures and unnecessary mocks. Consolidate overlapping tests around the strongest behavior checks. Repair valuable flaky tests instead of preserving their retry tax.
160	Treat deletions and consolidation as first-class deliverables. Follow the repository’s test-line budget; justify genuinely new coverage rather than padding a replacement suite. Never offset growth by deleting an independent safety contract.
161	Do not stop after easy deletions or a small first PR. Work through every in-scope subsystem. Keep a ledger of completed areas, removed duplication, remaining contract coverage and unresolved risks; resume from it until the campaign is complete. Do not chase a deletion percentage or add replacement tests just to keep the count up.
162	For each change, run the affected checks and demonstrate that the retained test fails for the relevant broken behavior when practical. Never delete the only useful regression guard to make a failure disappear. Keep platform and integration boundaries that protect distinct behavior.
163	Validate and land narrow PRs within the repository's existing review and merge rules. Continue until every in-scope area is checked or has a precise blocker. No releases.
164	```
165	
166	This is why the cleanup starts by reading the implementation, not sorting tests by runtime and deleting the slowest. Two similar-looking tests may protect different behavior; a very fast test may protect nothing useful. The question is what would break without it, and which remaining test would catch that break.
167	
168	## 2. Put each check at the right stage
169	
170	Not every check has to hold a PR open. We separated **the answer needed to merge this change** from **the broader proof needed to ship a release**.
171	
172	What runs when**Every push is not a full release rehearsal.**
173	Workflow designEvent-basedNot measured durations
174	**PR revision**Checks required for this change*→***Answer before merge**
175	Selected tests, lint, types, security and review.
176	**Push to main**Small regression and protocol guards*→***Catch immediate breakage**
177	Full-suite replay can be disabled; small guards remain.
178	**Scheduled worker**Broader validation of a named main revision*→***Repair failures; qualify releases**
179	Hourly main validation; full release checks on its own schedule.
180	Versioned workflow design; the live full-CI switch was not verified. Required release evidence must match the version being shipped.
181	
182	### Stop starting work that will be superseded
183	
184	A busy agent can push the next revision before the previous one finishes starting. The old run gets cancelled; the new run repeats setup. Those cancelled runs used compute without producing a useful result.
185	
186	Earlier in the campaign, the full main-push path gained a 90-second admission delay: a superseding push could cancel it before a Blacksmith runner started. That optimization preceded the separation of full validation from every main push. It was not a delay on PR feedback. The change.
187	
188	We also moved main’s CodeQL analysis to an **hourly** schedule. A successful, unchanged category could reuse its result for up to 24 hours; changed, stale, failed or incomplete categories ran again. PR and manual security checks stayed. Scheduling · Reuse rules.
189	
190	Moving a check changes when its answer is needed; it should not make a required answer optional.
191	
192	### Stop the job before paying for its setup
193	
194	A skip is worth more before the runner starts. The examples below trace six real workflow changes: a gate at the job condition avoids allocation and setup; a late check can only avoid the work after it. Put the decision at the earliest stage that has enough information to make it correctly.
195	
196	Execution path Stop unnecessary jobs before setup starts
197	IllustrativeExecution stagesNot measured frequencies
198	What happened**1** decide to start**2** start machine**3** check details**4** install & setup**5** run the check
199	#188600 Comment with a linkNo machine startsstop2345
200	#191007 PR checks already passedNo failure-report job startsstop2345
201	#95308 Comment does not request a reviewNo review is started12stop45
202	#189132 Scheduled PR checkSkip an unnecessary GitHub request12stop45
203	#191805 CodeQL result is still validNo new scan starts12stop45
204	selection Tests without a selection ruleEvery test still runs1234runs
205	A stop at step 1 avoids starting a machine. A stop at step 3 has already paid to start one, but avoids later work. Dark cells are reached; pale cells are skipped. These examples show where work stops, not how often it happens.
206	
207	### Do not rerun the full suite after every merge
208	
209	The full suite does not need to restart after every commit lands on main. The versioned workflow separates three jobs: give the PR its required answer before merge, run small guards on each main push, and let a scheduled worker check broader combinations on a named revision.
210	
211	Broader main validation runs hourly; full release validation has its own schedule. Full CI on every main push is opt-in in the source. Exact workflow and switch.
212	
213	A background worker needs a clear obligation: qualify a named revision, retain its results, and report failures to whoever can repair them. Do not silently treat an old green run as proof for a newer commit. Keep release gates attached to the version being shipped. That is the operational work required to move tests out of the author's immediate wait.
214	
215	We did not turn every background job into optional work. My rollout check was that releases did not suffer and full E2E runs did not reveal a new pattern of repeated regressions. That is an operational assessment, not a measured defect-rate claim.
216	
217	- Source and configuration detail
218	    
219	    At the article’s source revision, `OPENCLAW_CI_ON_PUSH=true` enables the full main-push path. The workflow retains small main-push guards, schedules main CI hourly, and schedules full release validation separately. This describes the versioned design; the live repository-variable value was not available to this audit. CI source · Release validation source.
220	    
221	
222	## 3. Stop paying for the same review twice
223	
224	ClawSweeper is OpenClaw's automated maintenance and code-review bot. It reviews pull requests and reports findings so contributors and maintainers can act on them. It is another consumer of compute and attention, not a free step outside the delivery process.
225	
226	ClawSweeper gives a new PR **one automatic review**. Follow-up reviews are requested, rather than automatically repeating the entire review after every push. Use a new review when the patch is ready for another pass or when a change needs fresh scrutiny; a request is not itself a passing review.
227	
228	Its local-review CLI lets us inspect a branch on our own machines without allocating an Actions runner. The standalone AutoReview skill offers another local review workflow. Local describes where the tooling runs, not an offline model: both use their configured model service.
229	
230	For a clean, committed branch, run this from a built ClawSweeper checkout, replacing the repository and path:
231	
232	```
233	pnpm run review -- --local-range \
234	  --target-repo owner/repo --target-dir ../your-repo \
235	  --base origin/main
236	```
237	
238	Or, with AutoReview installed, run from the repository you want reviewed:
239	
240	```
241	python3 "$HOME/.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview" \
242	  --mode branch --base origin/main
243	```
244	
245	The useful saving is avoiding redundant review starts and repeated findings while an author is still editing. Required CI, security checks and repository review rules remain. We did not move every review off CI, and no isolated review-cost percentage is claimed here.
246	
247	## 4. Test the change, not the entire repository
248	
249	Adaptive testing is the next step after cleanup: choose the remaining work from the change itself. Start with explicit ownership and dependencies. A changed test runs; a known production owner selects its related tests; shared, dynamic or uncertain paths widen the selection. A missing dependency record is a reason to run more, not evidence that nothing can break.
250	
251	For our TypeScript-heavy repository, we began with the changed files, their owners and the code importing them. A change to one component should not automatically start tests for every unrelated component and platform.
252	
253	For example, change a shared retry helper. Its own tests matter. So do tests of callers that import it. An unrelated UI component should not become relevant merely because it lives in the same repository. If we cannot establish the boundary safely, we run more.
254	
255	Adaptive testing · one TypeScript change**Change the code. Run the tests it can affect.**
256	IllustrativeOne changed fileDependency-based selection
257	Changed source`retry.ts`Shared retry helper
258	Own test`retry.test.ts`Proves retry behavior**Run**
259	Imports the helper`send.ts`Message sender
260	Caller’s test`send.test.ts`Proves sender behavior**Run**
261	Unrelated test`profile.test.ts`No path to the change**Skipped**
262	Selection appears at step 4**retry.test.tssend.test.tsprofile.test.ts**
263	1 / 4
264	**Start with the changed file.**
265	retry.ts changed. That is the input to the selector—not a reason to run everything.
266	Illustrative files · no model call
267	Teaching example, not a captured run. Current ownership and imports select tests. Missing or ambiguous inputs widen the run; they never justify a skip.
268	
269	Adaptive testing selects relevant tests, but smaller runs alone don’t prove complete coverage.
270	
271	### Keep selection boring, deterministic and testable
272	
273	We deliberately did not make this a complex AI scheduling system. Some teams use learned models or LLMs to choose tests. Our live path is ordinary code: the same revision, diff and rules produce the same selection. Every selected test should have a reason you can inspect. A model’s confidence is not a substitute for a dependency.
274	
275	**Backtest the selector against regressions.** Take an earlier bug, restore the revision before its fix, and replay the change through the selector. Check whether it includes the test that exposes the bug, then run that test and verify the expected failure. Include deleted files, shared helpers, fixtures and renamed modules—not just easy sibling-test examples. A missed regression is a rule to repair or a reason to widen the fallback. This is a repeatable validation recipe, not a claim that we have replayed every historical bug.
276	
277	### How we wired adaptive testing into CI
278	
279	The implementation is a planner in front of the existing test runner. It turns a Git diff into a list of existing test files, then gives those files to their normal execution jobs.
280	
281	**1. Start with an exact diff.** CI supplies the changed paths and comparison revision. Keep additions, deletions and rename information: removing a module can break its callers too. The planner also reads the current checkout and test inventory. A previous run’s dependency list is not a substitute for the code being tested now.
282	
283	**2. Find the owning tests, then the callers.** In `test-projects.test-support.mts`, we map known inputs to explicit test owners, look for sibling and directory tests, and follow reverse imports to tests that consume the changed code. Package aliases are resolved as well. The aggressive PR policy bounds how far some searches go; it is not an unlimited walk through the repository. Changes to mocked exports have extra rules to retain affected mock consumers.
284	
285	This is where the `retry.ts` example becomes real: select `retry.test.ts` because it owns the helper, and `send.test.ts` because its code consumes that helper. But an import graph cannot see every dependency. A test that reads a JSON fixture from disk needs an explicit owner rule or a recorded file dependency. “No import found” alone is not a reason to skip it.
286	
287	**3. Add the checks the diff does not get to remove.** `ci-changed-node-test-plan.mts` combines the result with the applicable policy checks and fixed smoke tests. Changed tests remain eligible to run. Tests with protected owners follow their own rules. The small unchanged-input shortcut described below applies only to reviewed Markdown tests in directory fallback—not to every test that passed last time.
288	
289	**4. Hand the selection to the existing runner.** The CI planner matches each selected file to its canonical test configuration, then constructs jobs with the appropriate runtime, setup and build requirements. Selecting the same file under Node and Bun still represents two executions. Missing executable owners or shard metadata cause the narrowed plan to be rejected, not treated as an empty successful test run. Broader coverage remains the fallback.
290	
291	**5. Make the decision inspectable.** The selector records reasons such as `explicit-owner`, `import-consumer`, `policy-watch` and `fixed-smoke`. That lets us trace a surprising selection back to a rule. We check those rules with focused selector tests and regression examples; for the recorded-dependency pilot, we also deliberately broke a fixture and verified that the affected test was selected and failed. A smaller green run, by itself, cannot prove that selection is correct.
292	
293	For local feedback, the repository exposes a changed-test command. Its defaults are not identical to the canonical CI planner; use the broader fallback when investigating a change that needs it:
294	
295	```
296	pnpm test:changed
297	# With broad fallback
298	OPENCLAW_TEST_CHANGED_BROAD=1 \
299	  pnpm test:changed
300	```

334	### What is implemented—and what still runs in shadow?
335	
336	The source-based selector answers a concrete question: which tests can this change affect? That works only as well as the relationships we can observe. We also explored whether past runs could add useful information—particularly when the source graph alone was incomplete.
337	
338	The first implementations are already merged. **Recording dependencies** means watching which code and files a test reads. **Learning a ranking** means using past changes and failures to predict which tests are most likely to fail on the next change. The first records a relationship; the second makes a prediction. Implementing both does not mean giving both permission to skip tests.
339	
340	Sampled CI already records test outcomes and dependencies. When compatible history is available, it also freezes a graph proposal and model scores before execution—without changing the scheduled tests. A new CLI audit collector adds separate outcome evidence without changing selection or displacing the ordinary history. This already records and checks predictions; it does not yet use them to skip tests.
341	
342	### Try the prediction without skipping the tests
343	
344	Say a proposed model picks 20 tests from a group of 1,000. We save its list, then run all 1,000 anyway. If a failing test is absent from the list of 20, we have found a miss. This is **shadow mode**: evaluate what a shortcut would have done without letting it remove protection. It costs the full run while we learn whether the prediction is trustworthy.
345	
346	Mozilla’s Firefox work used historical failures and relationships between changed files and tests to train an XGBoost model. Its shadow schedulers gave us a useful way to test a proposed shortcut before trusting it.
347	
348	Our experiments fed a small decision-tree model records of changed code, test dependencies and test outcomes. We trained on one set of examples, then checked new examples and entirely held-out code owners. A model doing well on familiar examples was not enough: some richer models missed regressions on held-out owners that the source graph caught.
349	
350	In use

353	
354	**Source-aware selection**
355	
356	Follow owners and imports to relevant tests. Unknown relationships widen the run.

361

363	
364	Nine reviewed Markdown tests can leave the directory fallback when their inputs match. Explicit ownership and imports still take precedence.

369

382	### Beyond TypeScript: select the right language owner
383	
384	Some unnecessary work came from crossing a language boundary for no reason. A TypeScript-only PR could start the independent Rust toolchain and workspace proof.
385

Rust configuration and sidecar fixture changes still select Rust; shared, deleted, unknown or incomplete inputs keep both owners. Manual and scheduled validation keep their existing rules.

390	## 5. Catch cheap failures locally; use faster tools
391	
392	A formatting error should not need a checkout, dependency install and remote test fleet before it reaches the author. Put the quickest useful checks where the change is made. Our recorded hook was pre-commit; the principle is to catch deterministic mistakes before the next remote round trip.
393	
394	Start with formatting, lint and a focused test command. Add type checking where its latency is practical. Keep the local path easy for people and agents to invoke, and run the required checks in CI too: a skipped hook is not proof that a patch is correct.
395	
396	Most of our code is TypeScript, so that toolchain was an obvious target. Our fast lint path uses **Oxlint**. The typechecker comparison below is a measured local invocation, not an end-to-end CI speedup.
397	
398	We retained `tsgo` as a fallback and for release validation. A faster tool belongs on the checks authors wait for after checking its compatibility; it does not automatically replace the required release check.
399	
400	The same approach applies outside TypeScript. A Go project can check formatting with `gofmt -l` and run `go vet` on the affected packages before its integration suite. A Rust project can run `cargo fmt --check` and check the affected package before a full platform matrix. These are examples readers can adopt, not changes we measured in this dataset; neither replaces the behavior tests.
401	
402	Measure each command on your own repository. There is no measured ESLint-to-Oxlint percentage in this dataset, and these tool gains cannot be added to the headline cost reduction.
403	
404	## 6. Stop rebuilding the same environment
405	
406	Once selection makes a test job small, its fixed setup can dominate. Time checkout, dependency restoration, compilation, fixture creation and the actual tests separately. A test that takes seconds can still sit behind minutes of preparation.
407	
408	### Fetch what the job needs
409	
410	**Blobless checkouts** keep Git history available while fetching file contents on demand. We need the base revision to compare changes, but not every historical file blob up front. This is different from a shallow checkout that may omit the merge base. Our timings-refit workflow combines full history with a blobless checkout. Check that your tooling gets a correct diff and that repeated lazy fetches do not erase the saving; no isolated checkout saving is measured here.
411	
412	### Make cache hits real
413	
414	A configured cache is not necessarily a useful cache. Check the restore result and the time still spent installing. Match reusable dependencies to their lockfile, toolchain and platform; do not reuse an incompatible build just because restoring it is fast. The same rule applies to package stores, compiler outputs and prepared test fixtures in other languages. Our CI cache policy also distinguishes trusted writers from restore-only or cache-off candidates; sharing setup must not let an untrusted job poison later results.
415	
416	### A smaller test run should need less setup
417	
418	Choosing two test files does not help much if their job still downloads and prepares everything needed by the entire suite. The runner has to fetch tools and files before it can execute a test.
419	
420	We replaced one **55.1 MB** all-in-one archive with a **30.0 MB** runtime package and a **0.48 MB** tooling package. A job restores the package it actually needs. These are package sizes, not a measured startup-time reduction. Source.
421	
422	### Trim platform setup, not the behavior under test
423	
424	On mobile and Mac, startup is not just a JavaScript import. It is simulator boot, signing, toolchains and platform packaging.
425	
426	Our iOS preparation uses SimSlim to disable selected simulator background services, including Spotlight and Family / Screen Time. It keeps capabilities the app needs, such as Siri and connectivity. Preparation waits for boot, applies the configuration and verifies it; the native harness keeps stock and SimSlim comparison arms.
427	
428	That is the principle: trim the environment without trimming the behavior under test. We have not reproduced a paired SimSlim speedup for this article, so there is no percentage attached to it. Preparation source · Qualification harness.
429	
430	### Load the tool once. Reset the test every time.
431	
432	In selected Vitest lanes, `isolate: false` lets files reuse a worker. The expensive runtime stays loaded, but each test must still reset its mocks, fixtures and handles. Process, database and end-to-end lanes that depend on isolation keep it. Narrowing a fixture can also avoid starting parts of the application the test never uses.
433	
434	The first measurement is case-execution time; the second is a whole invocation. Both preserve the stated cases, but they use different clocks and are not additive savings. Reuse the expensive preparation only where the next test still starts from the state it expects.

437	
438	### Sharding is not parallelism
439	
440	**Sharding** divides a suite into batches. **Parallelism** decides how many batches run at once. You can have 20 shards and run four at a time—or launch 20 separate machines.
441	
442	We had over-sharded. Too many runners repeated checkout, installation and startup before doing a small amount of useful work. The problem recurred. In September, I was still writing: “we need to be careful of oversharding … we overallocate boxes.”
443	
444	There are two separate decisions. First, put enough work in each job to make its setup worthwhile. Then distribute that work so the jobs finish at roughly the same time. A machine that finishes early cannot help a long-running job that already owns its files.

526	## Did the cheaper factory also get faster?

575	## CI needs continuous optimization too
576	
577	This is not a one-off cleanup. We now use agents to keep improving the CI process, not just to write the code that passes through it.
578	
579	Failures caught during final release validation feed back into that work. We use those regressions to tune the tests and CI checks. A green PR is not enough if the release process still finds a failure.
580

588

### What is implemented—and what still runs in shadow?

The source-based selector answers a concrete question: which tests can this change affect? That works only as well as the relationships we can observe. We also explored whether past runs could add useful information—particularly when the source graph alone was incomplete.

The first implementations are already merged. **Recording dependencies** means watching which code and files a test reads. **Learning a ranking** means using past changes and failures to predict which tests are most likely to fail on the next change. The first records a relationship; the second makes a prediction. Implementing both does not mean giving both permission to skip tests.

Sampled CI already records test outcomes and dependencies. When compatible history is available, it also freezes a graph proposal and model scores before execution—without changing the scheduled tests. A new CLI audit collector adds separate outcome evidence without changing selection or displacing the ordinary history. This already records and checks predictions; it does not yet use them to skip tests.

### Try the prediction without skipping the tests

Say a proposed model picks 20 tests from a group of 1,000. We save its list, then run all 1,000 anyway. If a failing test is absent from the list of 20, we have found a miss. This is **shadow mode**: evaluate what a shortcut would have done without letting it remove protection. It costs the full run while we learn whether the prediction is trustworthy.

Mozilla’s Firefox work used historical failures and relationships between changed files and tests to train an XGBoost model. Its shadow schedulers gave us a useful way to test a proposed shortcut before trusting it.

Our experiments fed a small decision-tree model records of changed code, test dependencies and test outcomes. We trained on one set of examples, then checked new examples and entirely held-out code owners. A model doing well on familiar examples was not enough: some richer models missed regressions on held-out owners that the source graph caught.

In use

**Source-aware selection**

Follow owners and imports to relevant tests. Unknown relationships widen the run.

**Declared fixture inputs**

Record file reads the import graph cannot see, and retain the tests affected by those inputs.

**Unchanged-input reuse**

Nine reviewed Markdown tests can leave the directory fallback when their inputs match. Explicit ownership and imports still take precedence.

Implemented · shadow mode

### Record predictions; keep the tests running.

**Historical graph proposals**

Compare compatible prior dependency records with the current change. Record the proposed subset without changing the run.

**Checked-in model scoring**

A small local tree records scores when compatible history is available. It cannot skip or reorder tests.

The dependency recorder had its own failure. A test read a fixture straight from disk; the import graph never saw that file. We declared it with Vite’s `addWatchFile`, then deliberately broke the fixture to check that the test was selected and failed on Node and pinned Bun.

Next, we’re experimenting with learned test selection and improving how we measure what gets skipped—and whether failures still get caught.

### Beyond TypeScript: select the right language owner

Some unnecessary work came from crossing a language boundary for no reason. A TypeScript-only PR could start the independent Rust toolchain and workspace proof.

We now compare the exact PR revisions to the TypeScript and Rust input lists. If the change belongs only to TypeScript, the independent Rust proof does not start. Rust configuration and sidecar fixture changes still select Rust; shared, deleted, unknown or incomplete inputs keep both owners. Manual and scheduled validation keep their existing rules.

One recorded Rust job took **81 seconds**. That identifies work an eligible change can avoid; it is not an 81-second reduction in the time to finish the whole PR. Rust owner-selection change.

## 5. Catch cheap failures locally; use faster tools

A formatting error should not need a checkout, dependency install and remote test fleet before it reaches the author. Put the quickest useful checks where the change is made. Our recorded hook was pre-commit; the principle is to catch deterministic mistakes before the next remote round trip.

Start with formatting, lint and a focused test command. Add type checking where its latency is practical. Keep the local path easy for people and agents to invoke, and run the required checks in CI too: a skipped hook is not proof that a patch is correct.

Most of our code is TypeScript, so that toolchain was an obvious target. Our fast lint path uses **Oxlint**. The typechecker comparison below is a measured local invocation, not an end-to-end CI speedup.

We retained `tsgo` as a fallback and for release validation. A faster tool belongs on the checks authors wait for after checking its compatibility; it does not automatically replace the required release check.

The same approach applies outside TypeScript. A Go project can check formatting with `gofmt -l` and run `go vet` on the affected packages before its integration suite. A Rust project can run `cargo fmt --check` and check the affected package before a full platform matrix. These are examples readers can adopt, not changes we measured in this dataset; neither replaces the behavior tests.

Measure each command on your own repository. There is no measured ESLint-to-Oxlint percentage in this dataset, and these tool gains cannot be added to the headline cost reduction.

## 6. Stop rebuilding the same environment

Once selection makes a test job small, its fixed setup can dominate. Time checkout, dependency restoration, compilation, fixture creation and the actual tests separately. A test that takes seconds can still sit behind minutes of preparation.

### Fetch what the job needs

**Blobless checkouts** keep Git history available while fetching file contents on demand. We need the base revision to compare changes, but not every historical file blob up front. This is different from a shallow checkout that may omit the merge base. Our timings-refit workflow combines full history with a blobless checkout. Check that your tooling gets a correct diff and that repeated lazy fetches do not erase the saving; no isolated checkout saving is measured here.

### Make cache hits real

A configured cache is not necessarily a useful cache. Check the restore result and the time still spent installing. Match reusable dependencies to their lockfile, toolchain and platform; do not reuse an incompatible build just because restoring it is fast. The same rule applies to package stores, compiler outputs and prepared test fixtures in other languages. Our CI cache policy also distinguishes trusted writers from restore-only or cache-off candidates; sharing setup must not let an untrusted job poison later results.

### A smaller test run should need less setup

Choosing two test files does not help much if their job still downloads and prepares everything needed by the entire suite. The runner has to fetch tools and files before it can execute a test.

We replaced one **55.1 MB** all-in-one archive with a **30.0 MB** runtime package and a **0.48 MB** tooling package. A job restores the package it actually needs. These are package sizes, not a measured startup-time reduction. Source.

### Trim platform setup, not the behavior under test

On mobile and Mac, startup is not just a JavaScript import. It is simulator boot, signing, toolchains and platform packaging.

Our iOS preparation uses SimSlim to disable selected simulator background services, including Spotlight and Family / Screen Time. It keeps capabilities the app needs, such as Siri and connectivity. Preparation waits for boot, applies the configuration and verifies it; the native harness keeps stock and SimSlim comparison arms.

That is the principle: trim the environment without trimming the behavior under test. We have not reproduced a paired SimSlim speedup for this article, so there is no percentage attached to it. Preparation source · Qualification harness.

### Load the tool once. Reset the test every time.

In selected Vitest lanes, `isolate: false` lets files reuse a worker. The expensive runtime stays loaded, but each test must still reset its mocks, fixtures and handles. Process, database and end-to-end lanes that depend on isolation keep it. Narrowing a fixture can also avoid starting parts of the application the test never uses.

The first measurement is case-execution time; the second is a whole invocation. Both preserve the stated cases, but they use different clocks and are not additive savings. Reuse the expensive preparation only where the next test still starts from the state it expects.

## 7. Pack, balance and size the remaining work

### Sharding is not parallelism

**Sharding** divides a suite into batches. **Parallelism** decides how many batches run at once. You can have 20 shards and run four at a time—or launch 20 separate machines.

We had over-sharded. Too many runners repeated checkout, installation and startup before doing a small amount of useful work. The problem recurred. In September, I was still writing: “we need to be careful of oversharding … we overallocate boxes.”

There are two separate decisions. First, put enough work in each job to make its setup worthwhile. Then distribute that work so the jobs finish at roughly the same time. A machine that finishes early cannot help a long-running job that already owns its files.

## Did the cheaper factory also get faster?

**Historical timing: through 4 November.** These charts predate the adaptive-selection rollout. They show why a lower bill is not enough to declare the delivery problem solved.

The first measures one feedback step. The second includes draft work, repeated checks, review and the wait to land. They belong beside one another—not added together, and not disguised as a count of agent tokens.

    **CI.** We enumerated all successful PR-triggered runs of the CI workflow on the third UTC day of each month from June to November, plus the partial day through 4 November, 14:11:47 UTC. Elapsed time is final non-skipped job completion minus workflow creation; parallel jobs are not summed. Median is the ordinary sample median, p90 the nearest-rank quantile. We filled 23 September–4 November, 14:11:47 UTC using fully paginated, complete daily GitHub merged-PR searches, retaining the same historical author accounts. ## CI needs continuous optimization too

This is not a one-off cleanup. We now use agents to keep improving the CI process, not just to write the code that passes through it.

Failures caught during final release validation feed back into that work. We use those regressions to tune the tests and CI checks. A green PR is not enough if the release process still finds a failure.

We will keep tuning sharding and packing as the test suite changes, and keep removing AI-written tests that add maintenance without catching useful failures. The point is to remove redundant work, not the checks that protect real behavior.

We are also starting to use Boat.dev, with their sponsorship, and building our own Mac Studio cluster. Slow background workloads can use a different pool from urgent PR checks. Moving the work does not make its cost disappear; it lets us fit the machine and deadline to the job.

We are also continuing to evaluate alternative test-selection tools and approaches. Changing providers or tools is one option; making the existing work smaller and better balanced is another.

I want to track **PR creation to merge** alongside release failures and compute use. That is how we can tell whether each change helps, rather than just making one chart look better.

I want to package the reusable parts into a skill and a standalone repository: inventory the tests, collect dependencies, replay selections, prove fallbacks and roll out conservatively. Neither is released yet.

The Desktop workflow is the slow one, running 20 to 34 minutes, with mac-x64 as the long pole at 28 minutes. I'm checking whether the native backend fetch hit the cache: the post-run cache step took 2:49 on mac-x64, which suggests it was saved rather than restored, a miss. But PR branches can only read caches scoped to their own branch, not main's, and Desktop doesn't seem to run on main.

The cache never warms on main, since Desktop doesn't run on main pushes, and PR branches can only read caches from their own branch or main. A warm-up job on push to main limited to changes in fetch-backend.mjs would fix that, and it would avoid a full build on every merge.

Next I'm working out what fetch-backend costs on each runner: about 2:38 on Windows, 5:00 on mac-x64, 2:06 on mac-arm64, and 1:09 on Linux. I still need to confirm from the logs whether the cache was actually hit. The npm ci steps are also heavy, at roughly 1:48 on Windows and 3:00 on mac-x64, so caching node_modules keyed on the lockfile and OS could help, and I want to check whether Electron is pulled in by npm ci.

I'm weighing whether the mac-x64 build could stay on Intel while still producing a smoke-testable app, and wondering if Rosetta on the arm64 runners could run the x64 build. I'm also looking at whether PRs only need the unpacked `--dir` target, since DMG creation on macOS is slow, though that might hide packaging problems until release.

I'm considering whether mac-x64 could run only when desktop or scripts/desktop files change, since Intel builds are the slowest and the platform risk from migration or package.json changes seems small. I'm also weighing whether Rosetta on the arm64 runners could stand in, though the comment says smoke tests must run natively, so that's a risk.

Next I'm looking at the CI checks job, which runs lint, typecheck, test, and build serially in about 2:40, and weighing whether splitting them into parallel jobs is worth the repeated npm ci cost (around 21 seconds each). The total wall time of roughly 3 minutes already seems fine, so caching the Next build output might be the more useful small win. I also want to check the latest failed run at 20 minutes and a few recent runs to see the typical duration spread.

I'm going to check the logs of a recent run to see whether the native backend cache is ever actually restored or if it's always a miss.

content.thinking:
I've found a bug: passing `--mac --x64` still builds arm64, because the config's mac target hardcodes both architectures and overrides the CLI flag. That means both mac jobs end up building both archs, which doubles the work. On top of that, the arm64 build packaged on the x64 job references a backend binary that isn't fetched there. The release also ends up with duplicate files from both mac jobs, since the merge step picks up both outputs.

I'm changing the plan here: the arm64 job on the mac-x64 runner has no darwin-arm64 backend to package, so it ships without one, and since both mac jobs upload files with the same names, whichever download finishes last decides what goes into the release. Dropping the hardcoded arch list from the mac target should fix both the correctness issue and the doubled packaging time.

I'm checking whether the cache job actually needs to run `npm ci`, since the setup-node npm cache only saves on a missed key. I also want to confirm that path filters get ignored for tag pushes, so the cache job won't misfire on releases.

I'm weighing whether the cache job really needs `npm ci`, since the setup-node npm cache only saves on a missed key and the install is what fills it. Cold installs take about 1:48 on Windows and 3:00 on mac-x64, so a warm cache might cut that roughly in half. The key is the package-lock hash, so PRs that touch the lockfile will miss anyway. I'm also wondering whether `fetch-backend.mjs` needs any node dependencies or only builtins, and the cache key can just hash that file. Saving `desktop/.cache` on PR misses costs about 2:49 on mac-x64 in the post step, which I'll need to account for.

Next I'm looking at the PR-side cache: restore-only on PRs with saves only from main, which keeps per-PR copies out of the 10GB repo cache limit. I also want to check the actual cache sizes with `gh cache list` to see whether eviction is what's causing the misses.

I'm estimating what the mac-x64 job would take after the fixes: npm ci and the backend fetch both get much shorter, and the post-step cache save disappears, so the long pole drops to roughly 14 minutes, with mac-arm64 near 8. I still want to check the cache list and what fetch-backend imports before trusting those numbers.

I'm checking whether fetch-backend skips the download when the file is already present, since the cache would only help if it does. The Go build cache should also carry over, so that part looks fine.

The mac target hardcodes both arm64 and x64, so each mac job packages both architectures, doubling packaging time and risking the x64 runner's artifact overwriting the real arm64 DMG. Checking cache sizes next.

I'm settling on the npm cache for now: the warm job's setup-node cache already writes the key that the build job will restore, so PR jobs hit main's entry and only save their own when the lockfile changes. That's simpler than restoring the cache manually.

cd /c/Users/mgsuk/.t3/worktrees/Moneo/t3-60edffa5-32d85c37dd0efb0a; gh pr create --base main --head t3/speed-up-ci --title "Speed up the Desktop workflow" --body-file - <<'EOF'
The Desktop workflow takes 20–34 minutes per pull request (last 9 runs). The long pole is mac-x64 at about 28 minutes. CI itself takes about 3 minutes and isn't changed here.

## What was slow (run 43977956957)

| mac-x64 step | Time | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Package | 10m 07s | Built **both** arm64 and x64 apps, DMGs and zips |
| Fetch the native backend | 4m 58s | Cache never hit |
| npm ci | 2m 57s | npm cache never hit |
| Post cache save | 2m 49s | Saved a 560 MB copy only this PR could read |
| Upload installers | 1m 28s | Twice the files |

1. **Both Mac jobs packaged both architectures.** `mac.target` listed `arch: ["arm64", "x64"]`, which overrides `--x64`/`--arm64`. The Intel job's arm64 app had no arm64 backend, and both jobs uploaded files with the same names into `merge-multiple`, so a release could ship whichever copy landed last. The CLI flag now picks the architecture.
2. **Caches never hit.** Pull requests can only restore caches from their own branch or `main`, and Desktop never ran on `main`. Every PR fetched the backend again and saved about 2 GB of caches no one else could use, which also pushed other entries out of the 10 GB limit. A `cache` job now fills `desktop/.cache` and the npm cache on `main` when `package-lock.json`, `fetch-backend.mjs` or this workflow changes, and weekly so the caches aren't evicted. The `build` job only restores them (`actions/cache/restore`).
